title: Bài sưu tầm 228 - Passage 2: The Architecture of Sleep: Why Marine Mammals Rest Half a Brain
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 228

The Architecture of Sleep: Why Marine Mammals Rest Half a Brain

Paragraph A. For land mammals, sleep requires surrendering awareness of the outside world for hours at a time. Yet for whales and dolphins, falling completely unconscious poses an immediate existential threat. Unlike fish that extract dissolved oxygen through gills, cetaceans breathe air at the water's surface through a conscious muscular effort; losing total awareness would quickly lead to suffocation or predation in open water.

Paragraph B. Evolution resolved this dilemma through a remarkable adaptation called unihemispheric slow-wave sleep. Brainwave recordings demonstrate that dolphins can put one half of their cerebral cortex into deep, restorative sleep while the opposite hemisphere remains fully awake. Each half of the brain controls the opposite eye, meaning that as one side rests, the corresponding lid closes while the other stays open to scan the water ahead. After roughly two hours, the hemispheres swap roles.

Paragraph C. Neuroethologist Dr. Oleg Lyamin tested whether this split-brain state compromises alertness over long stretches. Monitoring bottlenose dolphins continuously for five days, he found they maintained swimming speed and reacted accurately to visual signals without any sign of mental exhaustion. Interestingly, dolphins swimming in groups consistently kept the open eye turned toward the rest of the pod, suggesting that maintaining social contact is as vital as watching for sharks.

Paragraph D. Not all marine mammals rely on half-brain rest exclusively. Northern fur seals display a striking behavioural switch depending on their surroundings: when hauled out safely on land, they sleep with both brain hemispheres simultaneously just like dogs or humans. Once they enter the ocean for months-long foraging trips, however, they float on one side with a flipper paddling slowly, shifting immediately into unihemispheric mode until they return ashore.

Paragraph E. Another puzzle concerns rapid eye movement (REM) sleep—the dreaming stage accompanied by temporary muscle paralysis in humans. Researchers have struggled to detect clear REM signatures in captive dolphins, likely because full-body relaxation at sea would result in drowning. Some biologists suspect brief nocturnal muscle twitches observed in resting whales may represent a compressed substitute for REM, though others argue cetaceans abandoned that stage altogether millions of years ago.

Paragraph F. Remarkably, half-brain sleep is not confined to the oceans. Lightweight brain sensors attached to great frigatebirds crossing the Pacific revealed that they too shut down one hemisphere mid-flight while soaring on thermal updrafts. Yet a crucial difference remains: these airborne birds snatch less than an hour of total rest per day while aloft, catching up on deep bilateral sleep once they reach an island perch, whereas dolphins operate permanently on split-brain cycles.

Paragraph G. Studying how one half of a dolphin's brain clears cellular waste without halting vital movement has drawn interest from human sleep clinics. While human night-shift workers suffer severe cognitive impairment when forced to stay awake, marine mammals appear to avoid toxin buildup through rhythmic hemispheric alternation. Researchers hope that decoding this internal housekeeping mechanism could eventually inspire treatments for chronic sleep deprivation, though translating an aquatic adaptation to human neurology remains a distant goal.

groups.instructions:
Reading Passage 228 has seven sections, A–G.

groups.title: Questions 20–21
groups.instructions:
Choose TWO letters, A–E.
Write the correct letters in boxes 20 and 21 on your answer sheet.

Which TWO claims are made about unihemispheric sleep and human research in Section G?
options: A. Human shift workers already use brief half-brain naps successfully.
B. Dolphins manage to remove biological waste while remaining partly active.
C. Marine mammal sleep patterns have already cured severe insomnia in trials.
D. Halting all physical movement is essential for human brain detoxification.
E. Adapting this marine mechanism to human medicine is still far from practical use.

q14.text: an animal that alters its sleeping method according to its physical location

steps: Đoạn D: Hải cẩu lông phương Bắc ngủ cả 2 bán cầu khi lên cạn, nhưng chuyển ngay sang ngủ 1 bán cầu khi ra biển.
Kết luận: Chọn D.

q15.text: the biological reason why total unconsciousness is hazardous for whales

steps: Đoạn A: Cá voi phải chủ động nổi lên thở không khí bằng nỗ lực cơ bắp; mất ý thức hoàn toàn sẽ dẫn tới ngạt thở.
Kết luận: Chọn A.

q16.text: a comparison showing differences in daily rest duration between flying and swimming species

steps: Đoạn F: Chim cướp biển ngủ chưa tới 1 tiếng mỗi ngày khi bay (rồi ngủ bù khi đậu), khác với cá heo dùng ngủ nửa não vĩnh viễn.
Kết luận: Chọn F.

q17.text: experimental proof that continuous swimming with split sleep does not impair alertness

steps: Đoạn C: Thí nghiệm 5 ngày liên tục của Dr. Oleg Lyamin cho thấy cá heo giữ nguyên tốc độ và phản xạ tín hiệu thị giác không suy giảm.
Kết luận: Chọn C.

q18.text: uncertainty over whether a particular stage of sleep exists at all in cetaceans

steps: Đoạn E: Tranh cãi xem các cơn giật cơ ban đêm có phải là dạng REM rút gọn hay cá heo đã bỏ hẳn giai đoạn REM.
Kết luận: Chọn E.

q19.text: an explanation of how brain measurements reveal simultaneous rest and wakefulness

steps: Đoạn B: "Brainwave recordings demonstrate that dolphins can put one half... into deep, restorative sleep while the opposite hemisphere remains fully awake."
Kết luận: Chọn B.
Đoạn G: Cá voi/cá heo đào thải chất thải tế bào qua luân phiên bán cầu mà vẫn duy trì vận động (clears cellular waste without halting vital movement).
Kết luận: Chọn B (trong cặp B, E).
Đoạn G: "translating an aquatic adaptation to human neurology remains a distant goal."
Kết luận: Chọn E (trong cặp B, E).
Đoạn B: "Each half of the brain controls the opposite eye... while the other stays open..."
Từ cần điền: eye.
Đoạn C: "kept the open eye turned toward the rest of the pod" (their companions ↔ the rest of).
Từ cần điền: pod.
Đoạn D: "when hauled out safely on land, they sleep with both brain hemispheres simultaneously".
Từ cần điền: land.
Đoạn E: "full-body relaxation at sea would result in drowning" (would risk ↔ would result in).
Từ cần điền: drowning.
Đoạn F: "these airborne birds snatch less than an hour of total rest per day while aloft" (while flying ↔ while aloft / airborne).
Từ cần điền: birds.
